1401.title: Singing scripture
1401.hook: the Guru Granth Sahib is sung in set musical modes
1401.howItsDone: In gurdwaras, ragis sing hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib in the ragas named in its headings, often with harmonium and tabla, while the congregation sits and listens or sings along.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was nitnem: the Sikh daily round of set prayers, opening with Japji. Your line was the daily prayers.

Turn past the opening prayers of the Guru Granth Sahib, and look at the heading over the next hymn. In a novel, a heading gives you a chapter, or a topic. This one gives you a tune: Sri Raag. Then it tells you which Guru is speaking. Then the words. Before the meaning, the music. Page after page, the headings change: Raag Gauri, Raag Asa, Raag Sorath. The scripture is laid out like a songbook, because that's how it's meant to be heard. Five days ago, kirtan meant a room singing names back and forth. Today, the same word, and a different thing: scripture, sung.
screen: `A HEADING THAT GIVES A TUNE.` → `BEFORE THE MEANING, THE MUSIC.` → `LAID OUT LIKE A SONGBOOK.`

segments.voice: In Sikh life, kirtan is the singing of gurbani, the Guru's word: the hymns of the Guru Granth Sahib, sung in the musical modes, the ragas, that the scripture itself names. A raga is more than a scale. In Indian music, tradition ties each raga to a mood, and often to a time of day or a season. So when the heading names a raga, it's saying how the words should feel when they reach you. Tradition tells that Guru Nanak traveled with a Muslim musician, Bhai Mardana, who played the rebab, a stringed instrument, while the Guru sang. From the beginning, in the Sikh telling, the word came with music. In a gurdwara today, singers called ragis sit before the Guru Granth Sahib, often with harmonium and tabla, and sing its hymns. They don't bring new words; the words are the scripture. What changes is the singing. And the scripture speaks of this itself. In a hymn of Guru Arjan, the fifth Guru, a line says, in paraphrase, that in this dark age, kirtan is foremost. In Sikh teaching, the Guru Granth Sahib is the living Guru. So to sing it is not to perform about the Guru. It's to let the Guru's own words be heard the way the pages ask. A sentence read once is gone. A sentence sung comes back on its own, in the shower, in traffic, at night. Sung scripture goes home with you.
screen: `THE GURU'S WORD, IN RAGA.` · `A RAGA CARRIES A MOOD.` · `MARDANA'S REBAB, NANAK'S VOICE.` · `NO NEW WORDS: THE WORDS ARE SCRIPTURE.` · then, large: `IT GOES HOME WITH YOU.`

segments.voice: Listen to the sounds around you as if they were music: the hum of a fridge, a car, your own breath. Then bring to mind one line, from any source, that you know because it was sung, and notice how it arrives, tune first, then words.

Your line: sung scripture. A melody always brings its words along with it. See you tomorrow.

1402.title: Holy company
1402.hook: Sikhs stress the company of the good
1402.howItsDone: Sikhs gather as the sangat at the gurdwara to hear and sing the Guru Granth Sahib, then sit together in rows to share langar, a free meal served by volunteers; keeping good company is treated as part of spiritual life.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was kirtan: the Guru Granth Sahib sung in the ragas its own pages name. Your line was sung scripture.

Shoes off at the door. Head covered. Inside a gurdwara, people sit on the carpeted floor facing the Guru Granth Sahib. A banker sits beside a taxi driver. A grandmother sits beside a student straight from the gym. Nobody has a better seat. Later, in the kitchen hall, they sit again in rows on the floor, served the same simple meal by volunteers who may have sat beside them an hour ago. Who you sat with matters here, maybe more than how long you stayed. Sikhs have a word for the people in that room, and for what being among them does to a person.
screen: `SHOES OFF, HEAD COVERED.` → `NOBODY HAS A BETTER SEAT.` → `WHO YOU SAT WITH MATTERS.`

segments.voice: The word is sangat: company, the gathering, the congregation. At a gurdwara, the sangat is everyone who has come: the singers, the cooks, the visitors, you. Sikhs speak of the sadh sangat, the company of the holy, and the Guru Granth Sahib praises it. One whole section of the Sukhmani Sahib, a long hymn by Guru Arjan, praises that company line after line. In plain paraphrase: in the company of the holy, the face grows bright, the dirt on the mind is washed away, pride falls off, and the Name of God comes easily. Notice the claim. Not only that good people are pleasant to be around, but that company changes you. You become, a little, like the people you sit with. So for Sikhs, choosing your company isn't a social detail. It's part of the practice, like rising early or singing the hymns. And the sangat isn't a crowd you watch. It's a body you join. You sing with it, cook with it, sweep with it, sit in its rows to eat. The word travels beyond the gurdwara, too. A family might say the sangat helped them through a funeral. A visitor might hear: the sangat is your family now. Strip away the language and the question is plain, and sharp. Whose company makes you more patient, more honest, more like the person you mean to be? And whose quietly pulls the other way? Sikhs answer the first part with a place and a people: come and sit with the sangat.
screen: `SANGAT: THE COMPANY, THE CONGREGATION.` · `SADH SANGAT: THE COMPANY OF THE HOLY.` · `COMPANY CHANGES YOU.` · `A BODY YOU JOIN, NOT A CROWD YOU WATCH.` · then, large: `COME AND SIT WITH THE SANGAT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person in whose company you become a little better: kinder, calmer, more honest. Hold their face for a moment, and notice what changes in you as you picture sitting beside them. If you pray, give thanks for them; if you don't, simply be glad they exist.
Sangat. The company, the congregation, in the Sikh tradition. Sadh sangat is the company of the holy, the people whose presence washes the mind. Today's word.

1403.title: Sitting and forgetting
1403.hook: Zhuangzi's Yan Hui "sits and forgets" everything, even himself (Zhuangzi 6)
1403.howItsDone: Readers of the Zhuangzi meet zuowang in the story of Yan Hui and Confucius, and some Daoist practitioners treat sitting and forgetting as a meditation: sitting still and letting thoughts, senses and self-concern fall away.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was sangat: the Sikh company of the holy, where nobody has a better seat. Your line was good company.

A student walks up to his teacher with news. I'm making progress, he says. I've forgotten goodness and duty. The teacher nods. Good. But not yet. Some days later he's back. I've forgotten ritual and music. Good, says the teacher. But not yet. Then the student comes a third time, and this time the teacher is the one who's startled. The student is Yan Hui. The teacher is Confucius. And the book telling the story belongs to neither of them: it's the Zhuangzi, a Daoist classic. Today's word is what Yan Hui says on that third visit.
screen: `I'M MAKING PROGRESS.` → `GOOD. BUT NOT YET.` → `THE THIRD VISIT.`

segments.voice: On the third visit Yan Hui says: I sit and forget. In Chinese, zuowang. Confucius, the story says, looks startled and asks what that means. Yan Hui answers, in plain paraphrase: I let my limbs and body drop away. I dismiss my hearing and my sight. I leave my form behind, put away what I know, and become one with the great road that runs through everything. Then the turn. Confucius, the famous teacher, says: if you are one with it, you have no likes; if you are changed by it, you hold nothing fixed. You really are worthy. Please let me follow behind you. The teacher asks to become the student. Look at the order of what gets forgotten: first goodness and duty, then ritual and music. These aren't bad things; they're the very things Confucius taught. Yan Hui puts down even the good lists, and then the one keeping the lists. Readers take this more than one way. Some hear a method: a real sitting practice, emptying the mind until only stillness is left, and some later Daoists took it up that way. Others hear a joke with a point: here Zhuangzi puts words in Confucius's mouth, and lets the great teacher of rules bow to a student who has let the rules go. Either way, the story is gentle. Yan Hui doesn't fight his thoughts. He forgets them, the way you forget a coat on a warm day. You just stop carrying it.
screen: `I SIT AND FORGET.` · `BODY, SENSES, KNOWING: LET GO.` · `THE TEACHER ASKS TO FOLLOW.` · `EVEN THE GOOD LISTS GO DOWN.` · then, large: `PLEASE LET ME FOLLOW BEHIND YOU.`

segments.voice: Your mind will offer a list: things to do, things you forgot, things you should have said. Don't fight it and don't finish it; just notice, a list, and set it down like a bag. Let the body be heavy, let sounds come and go unnamed, and if another list arrives, set that one down too.
Zuowang. Sitting and forgetting, from the Zhuangzi: letting go of body, senses and knowing, until only the great road is left. Today's word.
Your line: sit and forget. Nothing to achieve here, only less to carry. Same time tomorrow.

1404.title: Qigong in the park
1404.hook: slow, breathing movement to cultivate qi, practiced in parks across China
1404.howItsDone: People practice qigong alone or in groups, often outdoors in the early morning: a sequence of slow movements coordinated with the breath, done with relaxed attention, sometimes led by a teacher and sometimes from memory.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was zuowang: Yan Hui sat and forgot, and Confucius asked to follow him. Your line was sit and forget.

Early morning, a city park in China, the air still cool. Under the trees, a few people stand in loose rows in ordinary clothes, one with a shopping bag at her feet. Their arms rise as slowly as smoke. They pause. The arms float down again. A small speaker plays soft music, and a man at the edge breathes out so long it's almost a sigh. Nobody is sweating. Nobody is counting reps. A jogger goes by, and next to them he looks like a film running too fast. Yesterday the stillness sat. Today it gets up and moves.
screen: `EARLY MORNING, A CITY PARK.` → `ARMS RISE AS SLOWLY AS SMOKE.` → `THE STILLNESS GETS UP AND MOVES.`

segments.voice: The word is qigong, in two parts. Qi is a Chinese word that covers breath, air, and the life that moves through a body. Gong means work, effort, skill built up over time. So qigong is something like working with qi: slow movement, steady breathing and a quiet mind, all done together. There are different schools, with names like the eight pieces of brocade, and teachers who disagree about the details. But they share a shape. Move slowly. Let the breath lead. Keep attention inside the movement, not ahead of it. Practitioners say this gathers and smooths the qi, the way a muddy pond settles. The breathing and stretching have old roots. The Zhuangzi, yesterday's book, mentions people who blow and breathe, spit out the old breath and take in the new, hang like a bear and stretch like a bird, all to live a long life. And here's the honest part: Zhuangzi doesn't fully approve. In paraphrase, he says the sage lives long without all the stretching, because the stillness is already inside. So even in its oldest mention, the practice comes with a question: is the movement the point, or the quiet underneath it? In the park, the answer looks like both. The arms move so the mind can rest. And slow turns out to be hard. Speed hides a lot. Slowness shows you every wobble, every held breath, every place you're hurrying to get somewhere else.
screen: `QI: BREATH, AIR, LIFE.` · `GONG: WORK BUILT UP OVER TIME.` · `HANG LIKE A BEAR, STRETCH LIKE A BIRD.` · `IS THE MOVEMENT THE POINT, OR THE QUIET?` · then, large: `SLOWNESS SHOWS YOU EVERY WOBBLE.`

segments.voice: Stand with feet about hip width and knees soft, or stay seated, and let your hands hang. Breathing in, let your arms float up in front of you to about shoulder height; breathing out, let them drift down, slower than feels normal, the breath setting the pace. After a few rounds, rest completely still and feel whatever is moving inside; go gently, and stop if anything hurts.
Qigong. Working with qi, the breath and life of the body, through slow movement, steady breathing and a quiet mind. Today's word.
Your line: slow movement. In the park, nobody is sweating and nobody is counting reps. Until tomorrow.

1405.title: Tai chi
1405.hook: a martial art turned moving meditation
1405.howItsDone: People practice tai chi by learning a form, a set sequence of slow, connected movements, usually from a teacher, and repeating it daily; some also train push hands with a partner to learn yielding and balance.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was qigong: arms rising as slowly as smoke in a morning park. Your line was slow movement.

Two people stand facing each other, forearms lightly touching. One pushes, gently. The other doesn't push back. She turns, gives way, and the push slides past her like water around a stone. Now he's off balance, and she has barely moved. This drill is called push hands, and it belongs to tai chi. From across a park, tai chi looks like the gentlest thing in the world: slow, floating, almost dreamy. But listen to the names of its movements. Single whip. Step back to repulse the monkey. Parry and punch. Under the slowness is a fighting art, softened until it became something people do to be still.
screen: `ONE PUSHES, THE OTHER GIVES WAY.` → `SINGLE WHIP. PARRY AND PUNCH.` → `A FIGHTING ART, SOFTENED.`

segments.voice: Tai chi is short for taijiquan. Quan means fist, a style of fighting. Taiji is older: it comes from the Book of Changes, the Yijing. A commentary there says, in paraphrase, that in the changes there is the taiji, which produces the two forms. Later readers took those two as yin and yang: dark and light, soft and hard, yielding and pressing, always turning into each other. The black-and-white circle is a picture of that turning. So tai chi is a fighting style named after the point where opposites meet and move. Its beginnings are wrapped in stories, a Daoist hermit, a family village, and the tellings don't agree. But the idea at its heart is in the Tao Te Ching, which Legge translated: "Man at his birth is supple and weak; at his death, firm and strong." The living thing bends. The stiff thing breaks. In push hands, stiffness is what gets you pushed over; softness, joined to good balance, stays standing. A tai chi form is one long, unbroken chain of movement: weight shifting from foot to foot, the waist turning, the arms following. Teachers say the body moves while the mind stays quiet and centered, like the hub of a turning wheel. Nothing jerks. Nothing hurries. The aim isn't to stop moving, but to stop rushing inside the movement.
screen: `QUAN: FIST. TAIJI: FROM THE YIJING.` · `YIN AND YANG, TURNING INTO EACH OTHER.` · `THE LIVING THING BENDS.` · `THE BODY MOVES, THE MIND STAYS CENTERED.` · then, large: `SUPPLE AND WEAK; FIRM AND STRONG.`

segments.voice: Stand with feet a little wider than your hips, knees soft, or sit and shift from one hip to the other. Slowly let your weight move into your right foot until the left grows light, then let it travel back through the middle and over into the left, arms drifting loose, no jerk at the turn. Keep the mind at the center while the weight moves; if standing isn't for you, watching a short tai chi form works too.
Tai chi. Taijiquan: a fighting art named for the point where yin and yang meet, now practiced as slow, unbroken movement with a quiet center. Today's word.

1406.title: Three daily checks
1406.hook: Zengzi examines himself three times daily: was I loyal, trustworthy, did I practice what I was taught? (Analects 1.4)
1406.howItsDone: People drawn to Confucian practice use Zengzi's three questions as a daily self-examination, often at the end of the day, sometimes keeping a journal of the answers.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was tai chi: a fighting art softened into moving stillness, where the one who yields stays standing. Your line was moving stillness.

If you could check only three things about your day before you slept, which three would you choose? Not your steps or your screen time. Three questions about who you were today. It's harder than it sounds. A list of ten is easy; ten lets you hide. Three makes you decide what actually matters. A student of Confucius named Zengzi made that choice, and his answer sits in the opening pages of the Analects, the book of Confucius's sayings. It's short enough to fit on a sticky note.
screen: `ONLY THREE THINGS. WHICH THREE?` → `TEN LETS YOU HIDE.` → `ZENGZI'S ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Here is Zengzi, in James Legge's translation: "I daily examine myself on three points." In plain words: First, in working for someone else, was I faithful? Did I give their task real effort, as if it were my own? Second, with my friends, was I true to my word? Third, what my teacher passed on to me, did I actually practice it? Look at what's missing. Nothing about success. Nothing about how others treated me. Nothing about feelings, or luck. All three are about the gap between what I owe and what I did, starting with the self, at close range, with the people right in front of you. And notice the word daily. Not once a year at a big turning point. Every day, small and plain, like brushing your teeth. There's a lovely puzzle in the third question. The Chinese is so compact it can be read two ways. Some readers take it as: did I practice what was passed on to me? Others: did I pass on to others anything I hadn't practiced myself? One is about the student, the other about the teacher, and one person can be both. Either way, the check is the same: do my words and my life match? The questions don't ask for guilt. They ask for honesty. Zengzi doesn't say what he does with the answers. Maybe that's the point: the checking itself is the practice.

1407.title: Li, ritual courtesy
1407.hook: Confucian ritual and courtesy shape the heart through the body
1407.howItsDone: In Confucian tradition li runs from formal rites, such as honoring ancestors and mourning, to everyday courtesy, such as greeting elders, bowing, and offering things with both hands, practiced so that respect becomes second nature.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was three daily checks: Zengzi's questions about being faithful, true to friends, and living what he was taught. Your line was three checks.

A small girl gets a present from her aunt. It's socks. Her face falls. Her father leans down and whispers: say thank you. She doesn't feel thankful. She says it anyway, a little sulky. Fake, maybe. But over the years she keeps saying it, and slowly the words reach inward. One day, without noticing, she means it. Which came first, the thanks or the thankfulness? One hunch says the heart has to change first, and the manners follow. Confucian teaching opens another possibility: the hands and the mouth can help lead the heart.
screen: `SAY THANK YOU.` → `SHE DOESN'T FEEL IT. SHE SAYS IT.` → `CAN THE HANDS LEAD THE HEART?`

segments.voice: The word is li. It can be translated ritual, propriety or courtesy, and it covers all three. Li is the great ceremonies, the offerings, the mourning rites. It's also how you bow, greet an elder, hand someone a cup. In the Analects, Confucius's student Yan Yuan asks him about ren, true goodness. The answer, in Legge's translation: "To subdue one's self and return to propriety, is perfect virtue." Then Confucius makes it concrete. In paraphrase: look at nothing, listen to nothing, say nothing, do nothing that is against li. It sounds rigid. It isn't meant to be empty. Another student asks what the root of li is, and Confucius praises the question. His answer, in paraphrase: in ceremonies, simple is better than lavish; at a funeral, real grief matters more than getting every detail right. Elsewhere he asks, more or less, what use is ritual to someone with no goodness in them? So li without a heart is hollow. But Confucian teachers read the form this way: the heart is trained through it. You bow, and the bow teaches respect. You stand when an elder enters, and standing makes room in you for them. Courtesy isn't a mask over who you are. Done again and again, carefully, it shapes who you become. This week's days share that thread: hymns sung, a sangat side by side, Yan Hui's sitting, the slow arms of qigong, tai chi's turning weight, Zengzi's questions. Put the body somewhere good, and the heart tends to follow.
screen: `LI: RITUAL, PROPRIETY, COURTESY.` · `RETURN TO PROPRIETY.` · `THE ROOT: REAL GRIEF OVER PERFECT DETAIL.` · `THE HEART IS TRAINED THROUGH THE FORM.` · then, large: `TO SUBDUE ONE'S SELF AND RETURN TO PROPRIETY.`

segments.voice: Choose one small courtesy, a greeting, a thank you, handing someone something with both hands, and rehearse it slowly in your mind: the person, your face, your hands, your voice, unhurried. Feel what it would be like to mean it fully; if you don't yet, that's fine, the form is allowed to go first.
